strengths: Well-motivated problem reformulation from MDP to POMDP perspective, clearly articulating the limitation of frame-independent processing in VLA models
Comprehensive experimental validation spanning simulation (LIBERO 4-suite, CALVIN) and real-world robot tasks (Mobile ALOHA) with consistent improvements across benchmarks
Thorough ablation studies isolating contributions of AVA module and state initialization, demonstrating each component's value (Tables 3-5)
Strong empirical results: 98.0% average SR on LIBERO (vs 96.8% baseline), 4.65 avg length on CALVIN (vs 4.28 baseline), with robust performance under perturbations
Effective qualitative visualizations (Figures 4-10) providing interpretable evidence of task-relevant attention focusing on critical visual features
Successful real-world demonstration on physical Mobile ALOHA robot showing practical applicability beyond simulation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: AVA module uses standard components (MLPs, self-attention, FFN); recurrent state formulation lacks formal theoretical justification for belief state approximation

Missing critical comparison with other history-modeling baselines: no comparison with Transformer-based temporal encoding, other RNN variants, or sequential visual encoders—a fundamental gap given the core contribution
No computational cost analysis: inference time overhead of recurrent computation not quantified; token pruning requires 50-60% retention to maintain performance, limiting practical benefits
Incomplete hyperparameter justification: T=4 frame sequence chosen for computational feasibility without ablation; L2 regularization weight appears ad-hoc; initial state r^{-1}=0 arbitrary
Real-world evaluation scale limited: only 30 trials for Mobile ALOHA (10 per object) vs thousands in simulation; 4 tasks tested—insufficient for statistical significance assessment
Incremental improvements in several settings: LIBERO single-task 99.2% vs 99.0% baseline; CALVIN shows marginal gains on some tasks—typical improvements are 1-2 percentage points
Missing failure analysis and error characterization: no discussion of when historical context is insufficient or method underperforms relative to baselines
Attention mechanism design choices underexplored: custom mask excluding language/instruction tokens from modulation lacks justification; FiLM modulation not compared with alternatives

strengths: Clear articulation of MDP limitations and POMDP motivation for VLA
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (LIBERO, CALVIN, Mobile ALOHA) with thoughtful ablation studies (Tables 3-5)
Interpretable attention visualizations demonstrating what the model focuses on during task execution
Validation on real robot platform beyond pure simulation
Generally well-written paper with clear presentation of methods and results
weaknesses: Empirical improvements are marginal and inconsistent: tied with RIFT-VLA on LIBERO (98.0%), worse than Seer on CALVIN (4.65 vs 4.28), with no statistical significance testing (no error bars/confidence intervals) despite multiple runs

Limited technical novelty: applying standard RNN + attention mechanisms to VLA is incremental; the soft attention weight computation (Eqs. 10-12) uses conventional FFN-based attention without architectural innovation
POMDP theoretical motivation appears post-hoc and disconnected from the actual method; the approach simply adds recurrent states, equivalent to standard RNN-based VLA without principled POMDP solving
Unfair baseline comparison: the OpenVLA-OFT architecture is modified with AVA module and recurrent initialization, confounding architectural changes with the recurrent mechanism contribution

Critical missing analysis: no computational cost discussion (inference latency/memory overhead), no hyperparameter sensitivity analysis despite multiple loss terms (λ, c, η, γ, τ), arbitrary zero initialization for recurrent state not justified
Real-world validation insufficient: single robot platform with only 4 tasks, mixed results across tasks without analysis of when/why method helps, no sim-to-real transfer analysis

Suspicious perfect alignment on LIBERO (exactly 98.0% matching RIFT-VLA) with more variable results on LIBERO+ suggesting potential overfitting; inconsistent results across backbones (Table 3: 94.5% vs 96.2%) indicate instability
Qualitative analysis limitations: only successful trajectories visualized, no failure case analysis, attention dynamics visualizations don't establish that model learns task-relevant patterns
Abstract oversells contribution claiming 'state-of-the-art' when results often match or underperform baselines (e.g., CALVIN case)
Token pruning study (Table 5) appears orthogonal to main contribution; performance drops contradict claimed focus on task-critical visual regions, suggesting a flaw in the core design principle

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies that VLA models lack temporal/historical context and articulates this through POMDP perspective
Sound technical approach: AVA module elegantly combines recurrent states with soft attention to dynamically modulate visual processing based on history
Comprehensive experimental validation: Multiple simulation benchmarks (LIBERO, CALVIN) plus real-world robot experiments (Mobile ALOHA) demonstrating broad applicability
Consistent empirical improvements: State-of-the-art results across benchmarks (98.0% vs 96.8% LIBERO, 99.2 vs 97.6 CALVIN single-task)
Thorough ablation studies: Table 4 convincingly demonstrates both AVA module and state initialization contribute meaningfully to performance
Excellent visualization and analysis: Qualitative evidence (Figures 3, 5) shows attention focuses on task-relevant regions; attention dynamics clearly visualized
Robustness demonstrated: Visual token pruning analysis (Table 5) shows method maintains 97.3% performance with 70% token removal
Strong reproducibility: Extensive implementation details, hyperparameters, and training procedures in appendices enable verification and reproduction
Clear presentation: Well-written with helpful diagrams (especially Figure 2) making framework accessible and contribution clear
weaknesses: Limited individual component novelty: Recurrent states and soft attention are well-established techniques; main contribution is their specific application to VLA rather than fundamentally new methods
Modest improvements in some cases: Some performance gains are marginal (1-2%); no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals provided to assess reliability
Missing computational cost analysis: No inference time overhead quantification, training time comparison, or memory analysis for recurrent state maintenance despite claims about efficiency
Narrow real-world evaluation scope: Single robot platform (Mobile ALOHA), only 4 tasks, some with limited demonstrations (30-450); no cross-robot or cross-embodiment validation
Recurrent state initialization underexplored: Initialization strategy (zero embedding) not thoroughly analyzed; no sensitivity study or failure mode discussion; minimal ablation coverage
Limited theoretical depth: POMDP motivation is good but lacks analysis of when/why historical context helps; no theoretical justification for specific attention design choices
Generalization not thoroughly examined: No cross-dataset evaluation; unclear which task types benefit most from historical context; limited failure case analysis
Unclear baseline fairness: Different methods may have different training data/compute budgets; experimental setup consistency across baselines not fully established
Visual token pruning analysis lacks mechanistic understanding: Shows robustness empirically (Table 5) but provides limited insight into what information is retained or why 70% pruning works
Missing ablations: No sensitivity analysis for recurrent state dimension, attention layer architecture, or loss coefficient λ; limited exploration of design space

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies and addresses the limitation of VLA models processing frames independently, with sound POMDP-based theoretical grounding
Comprehensive experimental validation: Consistent improvements across three benchmarks (LIBERO, CALVIN, Mobile ALOHA) with thorough ablation studies (Tables 4-7) demonstrating component effectiveness
Rigorous ablation design: Tables 4-7 effectively isolate contributions and control for confounding factors like training compute, with matched training settings comparison
Insightful behavioral analysis: Figure 4 visualization of attention dynamics and Figures 7-11 showing learned focus patterns across viewpoints provide good interpretability
Clear presentation and reproducibility: Well-structured paper with detailed implementation details, comprehensive appendices, open-source base models, and good figure quality
Practical efficiency: LoRA-based optimization keeps parameter overhead <1% of base model
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: The AVA module uses standard components (MLPs, cross-attention, softmax). While the application to recurrent VLA is novel, the mechanism itself is relatively straightforward
Incremental improvements: CALVIN shows modest gains (98.2% vs 97.5%), LIBERO task-specific benefits vary significantly; 1-2% gains on several tasks may not justify added complexity

Incomplete computational analysis: No FLOPs or latency measurements reported; recurrent processing overhead not quantified; memory requirements for hidden states not analyzed; implications for real-time control unclear

Severely limited real-world validation: Only 4 Mobile ALOHA tasks with 30 demonstrations each; no real-world baseline comparisons; claims of 'real-world applicability' unsupported; all long-horizon results remain simulation-based

Hyperparameter tuning concerns: Different penalty coefficients for different benchmarks (c=0.2 for LIBERO, c=0.1 for CALVIN); state initialization provides minimal ablation benefit (97.4% vs 97.2%) yet is task-specifically enabled

Insufficient design analysis: No systematic study of history length; missing sensitivity analysis for key hyperparameters; no investigation of whether attention captures temporal dependencies vs. static features

Loose POMDP connection: While conceptually motivated, the connection between theoretical POMDP formulation (Eqs. 3-4) and actual attention mechanism is tenuous; POMDP serves more as post-hoc motivation than derivation foundation

Limited failure mode analysis: Figure 13 failure cases attributed to 'spatial belief errors' without deep investigation; no systematic study of when/why attention mechanism fails or whether it helps in failure scenarios
Temporal grounding not addressed: Method doesn't explicitly encode timestep information; unclear how model distinguishes recent vs. distant history in recurrent state

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three diverse benchmarks (LIBERO, CALVIN, Mobile ALOHA) combining simulation and real-robot validation demonstrates broad applicability
Systematic ablation studies (Table 4, appendix sections D.1-D.4) validating individual components showing thorough investigation of the approach
Well-motivated problem addressing the limitation that current VLA models ignore historical context in temporal reasoning for sequential manipulation
Detailed implementation transparency with explicit hyperparameters, training procedures, and architectural modifications supporting reproducibility
Effective attention visualizations (Figures 4, 7-11) demonstrating that the model focuses on task-relevant regions and providing interpretability
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core contribution reduces to adding standard recurrent states and self-attention to VLA models. The AVA module (Eqs. 7-11) is conventional multi-head attention applied to visual tokens without principled innovation

Weak POMDP connection: The POMDP framing (Eqs. 3-4) lacks rigorous theoretical grounding and appears post-hoc. The belief state is a standard RNN hidden state without POMDP-theoretic design constraints or information-theoretic objectives

Modest empirical improvements insufficient to justify added complexity: 1.2% on LIBERO (98.0 vs 96.8), unclear metrics on CALVIN, modest gains on Mobile ALOHA without error bars or statistical significance testing

Critical omission: No discussion of computational overhead (inference latency, memory cost, real-time feasibility) despite adding recurrent computation and attention mechanisms—essential for robotic applications

Incomplete baseline comparisons: Table 7 shows similar improvements under matched training settings, suggesting gains may derive from optimization differences rather than the core method. Limited comparison with other memory-augmented or recurrent VLA approaches

Ad-hoc loss function design: L2 penalty (Eq. 13) lacks theoretical justification; arbitrary hyperparameter choices (c=0.2, λ values) without sensitivity analysis. Penalizing mean attention could suppress legitimate task-critical patterns

Real-world validation limitations: Mobile ALOHA uses only 4 tasks with 30-60 demonstrations; suspiciously low baseline success rates raise implementation fairness concerns; no error bars, statistical significance, or multi-trial reporting

Insufficient failure analysis: Figure 13 failures lack mechanistic explanation. Statements about 'spatial belief errors' and 'perceptual inaccuracies' provide no systematic categorization or insights into when the method fails
Unsubstantiated generalization claims: 'Strong understanding and generalization abilities' asserted without out-of-distribution evaluation, unseen environments, or novel object/task categories

Missing practical considerations: No computational cost analysis, no sensitivity analysis for key hyperparameters (horizon T only in appendix), no code availability statement, no comparison with simpler temporal aggregation baselines

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly identifies and addresses a genuine limitation of existing VLA models that process frames independently without temporal context

Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple benchmarks (LIBERO, CALVIN, Mobile ALOHA) with both simulation and real-world robot deployment, demonstrating consistent improvements (98.0% vs 96.8% LIBERO, 84.1 vs 72.9 CALVIN)
Solid theoretical grounding through POMDP formulation that principally motivates recurrent state modeling and historical context preservation
Thorough ablation studies (Tables 4-5) clearly demonstrating the contribution of both state-based initialization and the Active Visual Attention module
Excellent visualization and analysis showing attention weights consistently focusing on task-relevant objects and regions across diverse manipulation tasks
Methodological rigor including robustness evaluation under controlled perturbations (LIBERO+), matched training settings comparison, and honest failure case analysis
Practical real-world validation on Mobile ALOHA robots strengthens claims beyond simulation benchmarks
Strong reproducibility with detailed implementation specifications, hyperparameters, training procedures, and sufficient detail for reproduction
weaknesses: Limited component-level novelty: recurrent temporal modeling and softmax attention are well-established techniques; the POMDP formulation doesn't yield fundamental algorithmic insights beyond standard RNN+attention combination

Computational overhead analysis insufficient: no inference time comparisons provided, memory cost of recurrent states not quantified, and claims about 'soft weights' reducing computation lack empirical evidence

Regularization design appears ad-hoc: L_ω penalty (Eq. 13) justified primarily for preventing weight dispersion, only c=0.2 tested without ablation on regularization strength, and matched-settings results suggest sensitivity
Incomplete failure characterization: Figure 13 shows failures but minimal analysis; fundamental challenges on long-horizon tasks not explored; deferred solutions suggest incomplete understanding
Unclear generalization scope: all experiments limited to manipulation tasks; applicability to other robotics domains (navigation, grasping) and task types not demonstrated

Matched training settings (Section D.1, Table 7) show gains diminish under controlled conditions, raising questions about whether improvements stem from architectural innovation or training protocol differences
Limited investigation of learned dynamics: recurrent state remains largely a black box with no visualization or analysis of how hidden representations evolve across trajectories
Modest improvements in single-task settings: LIBERO one-policy shows only +1.2% over best baseline (98.0% vs 97.4%); improvements are consistent but not transformative
No comparison with alternative temporal modeling approaches: missing comparisons to causal Transformers, temporal convolutions, or other sequence modeling methods
Soft weight analysis lacks task-level characterization: missing analysis of which task properties benefit most from dynamic attention or whether static attention suffices for certain tasks
